lessons.title: Logging in: who and where you are
lessons.summary: What Geiss-01 is, how you reach it, and two commands that confirm you landed in the right place.

blocks.text:
Geiss-01 is a shared computer in the lab with 8 powerful GPUs and about 190 GB of memory. You don't sit at it. You reach it over the network from your own laptop and type commands into a terminal: a window where you type a command, press Enter, and read what it prints.

You connect with `ssh` (secure shell), for example `ssh student@geiss-01`, and type your password. From then on, everything you type runs on Geiss-01, not on your laptop. This site skips the login and drops you straight into a practice copy.
The prompt at the start of each line tells you who and where you are: `student@geiss-01:~$` means user `student`, on the computer `geiss-01`, in the folder `~`. The `$` means it's waiting for you.

command.name: whoami
command.what: Prints the user name you are logged in as. Your files, jobs and permissions all belong to this name.

command.name: hostname
command.what: Prints the name of the computer you are on. When you have several terminals open, some on your laptop and some on the cluster, this tells you which is which.

try.text: Check which computer this terminal is on.

blocks.tip: Commands are case sensitive. `whoami` works; `WhoAmI` doesn't. Almost every Linux command is lowercase.

quiz.q: Your prompt reads `student@geiss-01:~/runs$`. What does `~/runs` tell you?
quiz.why: The part after the colon is the folder you're in. `~` is your home folder, so you're in the runs folder inside it.

lessons.title: GPUs and nvidia-smi
lessons.summary: What the GPUs are for, and how to see which ones are busy.

blocks.text:
A GPU (graphics processing unit) does thousands of small calculations at once. Structure prediction and design tools like ColabFold, Chai-1 and RFdiffusion need one; on a normal processor they would take days instead of minutes.

Geiss-01 has 8 GPUs, numbered 0 to 7, shared by everyone in the class and the lab. Before asking for one, it helps to see how busy they are.

command.name: nvidia-smi
command.what: Prints a table of the GPUs: each one's number, how much of its memory is in use, how busy it is, and which programs are running on it.

example.out:
| GPU  Name                  | Memory-Usage          | GPU-Util |
|   0  RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell |  71234MiB / 97887MiB  |    98%   |
|   1  RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell |      0MiB / 97887MiB  |     0%   |
example.note: GPU 0 is busy: most of its memory is used and it's at 98%. GPU 1 is idle. A GPU with memory in use and a process listed below the table belongs to someone's job.

try.hint: Type nvidia-smi (with the dash) and press Enter.

blocks.warn: Seeing a free GPU doesn't mean you can just use it. On Geiss-01 you ask Slurm for a GPU (lesson 5), and Slurm gives you one that nobody else is using.

quiz.q: In nvidia-smi, a GPU shows 0MiB memory used and 0% utilization. What does that mean?
options: Nobody is using it right now
It is reserved for the instructor
quiz.why: No memory in use and no work being done means the GPU is idle at the moment.

lessons.title: Loading software with modules
lessons.summary: Why software isn't there until you load it, and the module commands.

blocks.text:
Geiss-01 has many programs installed, sometimes several versions of the same one. If all of them were switched on at once they would clash. Instead, software is packaged as modules that you load when you need them.

Loading a module adds the program to your PATH, the list of folders the shell searches when you type a command name. Before you load it, typing the program's name gives `command not found`.

command.name: module
command.syntax: module avail | list | load NAME | unload NAME | purge
command.what: Manages which software is switched on in this terminal. The word after `module` says what to do.

flags: List every module you could load
Switch on that software (and the version shown, like colabfold/1.5.5)
Show what you have loaded now
Switch everything off and start clean

try.text: Load ColabFold, then check it's loaded.
try.hint: module load colabfold, then module list

blocks.tip: Modules last until you close the terminal or the job ends. Every new login, and every batch job, starts with nothing loaded, so job scripts load their modules at the top.

quiz.q: You type `colabfold_batch` and get `command not found`. What's the most likely fix?
quiz.why: The program is installed but not switched on in this terminal. Loading its module puts it on your PATH.

lessons.title: Conda environments
lessons.summary: Python tools live in their own environments. Here's how to switch them on and check which Python you're using.

blocks.text:
Python tools like ProteinMPNN and Chai-1 each need specific versions of many Python packages, and those versions often conflict. Conda solves this by giving each tool its own environment: a separate folder with its own Python and its own packages.

On Geiss-01, conda itself comes from a module, so you load that first.

command.name: conda
command.syntax: conda env list | activate NAME | deactivate
command.what: Lists environments, switches one on, or switches it off. Only one environment is active at a time; activating another replaces it.

flags: Show every environment; the active one has a *
Switch on that environment; its name appears in brackets before your prompt

try.text: Load anaconda, list the environments, and activate `proteinmpnn`.
try.hint: module load anaconda, then conda env list, then conda activate proteinmpnn

command.name: which
command.what: Prints the full path of the program that runs when you type NAME. `which python` tells you which environment's Python you're about to use.

try.text: Activate `chai` and check which python you'd run.
try.hint: module load anaconda, conda activate chai, then which python

quiz.q: `which python` prints `/opt/conda/envs/chai/bin/python`. Which environment is active?
quiz.why: The path goes through envs/chai, so that Python, with Chai-1's packages, is the one that runs.

lessons.title: Asking Slurm for a GPU
lessons.summary: Slurm hands out the GPUs fairly. srun gets you one to work on interactively.

blocks.text:
With many people sharing 8 GPUs, something has to decide who gets which one, so two jobs never fight over the same GPU. That something is Slurm, the job scheduler. You tell Slurm what you need; it finds free resources, reserves them for you, and gives them back when you're done.

The resources Slurm hands out are GPUs, memory (RAM), CPU cores and time. Together they're called an allocation, and a running allocation is a job.

command.name: srun
command.what: Asks Slurm for resources and runs COMMAND inside them. With `--pty bash`, the command is a new shell you can type in, so you get an interactive session on the GPU.

flags: How many GPUs (here 1). Leave it out and you get none
How much RAM for the job. Leave it out and you get 16G for each GPU (4G with no GPU)
Hours:minutes:seconds before Slurm ends the job
Which queue: gpu (up to 2 days) or short (up to 1 hour)
Connect the job to your keyboard and screen
The program to run: a shell, so you can type commands in the job

try.text: Get an interactive session with one GPU.

command.name: exit
command.what: Leaves the interactive job and gives the GPU back. Always exit when you're done; an idle session still holds a GPU someone else could use.

try.text: Get a GPU session, then give it back.

tasks.text: Start a session with one GPU

command.name: sinfo
command.what: Lists the partitions (queues) and whether their nodes are idle, partly used (mix) or fully used (alloc). TIMELIMIT is the longest job each partition allows.

quiz.q: You ran `srun --pty bash` with no other options. Can you run ColabFold in that session?
options: Yes, every job gets a GPU
No, you asked for no GPU
quiz.why: Without --gres=gpu:1, Slurm gives you a job with no GPU. GPU tools will stop with a 'no GPU' error.

lessons.title: Sizing a request, and cleaning up
lessons.summary: Run one command on a GPU, ask for the right memory and time, and find jobs you forgot.

blocks.text: Leave out `--pty bash` and srun runs a single command in the allocation, prints its output, and gives everything back as soon as the command finishes. Handy for a quick check.

try.text: Run `nvidia-smi` once on a GPU through Slurm.

blocks.text: Ask for what the work needs: enough that it doesn't get killed, not so much that you hold resources others are waiting for. Memory is written with a unit: `--mem=48G` is 48 gigabytes. Geiss-01 has about 190 GB for the whole class, and in this course each student can hold at most 2 GPUs and 48 GB at a time. Time is `hours:minutes:seconds`, or `days-hours:minutes:seconds` for long jobs.

flags: Too little and the job is killed: OUT_OF_MEMORY
Too little and the job is stopped: TIMEOUT
The gpu partition allows up to 2 days
Only if the program actually uses more than one

try.text: Start an interactive session with 2 GPUs, 48 GB of memory and 3 hours.

command.name: squeue
command.what: Lists your jobs that are waiting (PD, pending) or running (R). A session you forgot to exit shows up here, still holding its GPU.

command.name: scancel
command.what: Ends one of your jobs and frees its resources. Get the JOBID from squeue.

try.text: You left a session running yesterday. Find it and cancel it.
try.hint: squeue --me shows the JOBID; then scancel 47790

quiz.q: Your job needs about 2 hours. Which time request is best?
quiz.why: 2.5 hours covers the work with some margin. Too short and it times out; 2 days holds the slot far longer than needed; the default here is only 1 hour.
